questions.prompt: A container writes to `/data` and gets `OSError: [Errno 30] Read-only file system`. The host directory is mode 777 and the process runs as root. What do you check first?
choices: SELinux or AppArmor labels on the directory
Whether the disk is full
The options of the mount that `/data` resolves through: `ro` is a per-mount flag set by `-v ...:ro` or `readOnlyRootFilesystem`, and no permission bit overrides it
The umask of the process
questions.explanation: EROFS comes from the mount, not from the file. The path walk ends on a row of the mount table whose options contain ro; chmod, ownership and umask are never consulted. findmnt -T /data or mountlens which /data shows the row and the flag.

questions.prompt: In a `/proc/self/mountinfo` row, what does a `root` field (field 4) other than `/` tell you?
choices: The row is a bind mount: only that subtree of the source filesystem is visible at the mount point, so a path there maps to root plus the relative path on the source
The filesystem was mounted read-only
The mount belongs to another mount namespace
The filesystem is corrupted and was remounted
questions.explanation: Field 4 is the subtree of the source filesystem this mount shows. A plain mount shows the whole filesystem, so its root is /. Docker volumes, hostPath, subPath, emptyDir and the masked /proc entries are binds, and their root is the directory or file on the source.

questions.prompt: `df -h` shows the data volume 41% used, yet the application keeps failing with `No space left on device`. Which check settles it?
choices: `du -sh /` to find the biggest directory
`lsblk` to confirm the disk size
`mount` to see whether the volume is read-only
`df -i` (or `mountlens usage`): a filesystem with free blocks but no free inodes refuses every new file with ENOSPC, and df -h cannot show it
questions.explanation: statvfs reports blocks and inodes separately and creat() needs one of each. Millions of small files exhaust the inode table long before the blocks run out; deleting a few large files frees blocks and changes nothing. df -i or the IUSE% column names the resource that is actually gone.

questions.prompt: Inside a container started with `docker run --read-only`, `mountlens overlay` shows an `upperdir` for `/`. Why is the root still read-only?
choices: The upperdir sits on a read-only disk on the host

`--read-only` sets the `ro` flag on the overlay mount itself: the writable layer exists on the host, but this mount point refuses writes, which is exactly what makes `ro` a per-mount flag rather than a property of the layers
Docker deletes the upperdir after the container starts
overlayfs is always read-only unless `--privileged` is given
questions.explanation: An overlay without upperdir is read-only by construction. One with upperdir and an ro mount flag is what --read-only produces: the runtime remounts the rootfs with MS_RDONLY after it is assembled. The flag lives in field 6 of the mountinfo row while the superblock options still say rw.

questions.prompt: You mount a new disk on the host at `/mnt/disk2` while a container started with `-v /mnt:/mnt` is running. Inside the container `/mnt/disk2` is an empty directory. Why?
choices: The container must be restarted to re-read /etc/fstab
Docker caches directory listings for the lifetime of the container

The volume row has the default `rprivate` propagation: it belongs to no peer group, so new mounts under the host's `/mnt` are not propagated. `-v /mnt:/mnt:rslave` or `mountPropagation: HostToContainer` would receive it
The new disk must be formatted with overlayfs to be visible in containers
questions.explanation: Mount propagation is decided per row by the shared:N and master:N tags. A private row receives nothing; a slave row receives mounts from its master peer group. Runtimes default volumes to rprivate, and changing propagation requires a new container.

questions.prompt: `mountlens shadowed` lists a tmpfs at `/mnt/scratch` hidden under a later bind mount at the same path. What is true about the tmpfs?
choices: Its memory is still allocated and `df` still counts it, but no path reaches its files until the covering mount is unmounted
The kernel unmounted it automatically when the second mount was made
Its files were merged into the bind mount like an overlay layer
It is visible only to processes running as root
questions.explanation: Mounting on a directory that is already a mount point stacks the new mount on top. The old row stays in the table with its data allocated; the path walk only ever reaches the topmost mount. umount of the covering mount brings the tmpfs back, which is why df and du disagree until then.
